GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: watch where Q, the tip of the triangle on CD, meets the circle through A, B and S.
How to play: Drag S, C or D, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes for names, angle marks and the hint triangles, or press Reset to start again.
Look for the math

The original page still shows the Java applet behind a "browser is not set to run Java applets" notice; its two applet tags are present in the page source. It calls this picture a variation of an equilic quadrilateral. The surprising point is where the tip of one isosceles triangle lands on the circle through A, B and S.

The construction

A and B are fixed on a circle. S can be dragged freely. C is placed on the line from B towards S and D on the line from A towards S, both at the same distance from their starting corner, so AD = BC always. The applet then measures the angle at S with the law of cosines, angle(S,A,B) = acos((SA² + SB² − AB²) / (2·SA·SB)), and builds Q as the apex of the isosceles triangle on CD with angle CQD = angle BSA. Tick "Construction" to see those two equal angles and the matching side marks.

What the page says, and what is true

Assume in a quadrilateral ABCD AD = BC, S the intersection of AD and BC. Let Q be the apex of an isosceles triangle CDQ drawn away from AB with ∠CQD = ∠BSA. Then S is the midpoint of the arc of the circumcircle of ΔABS containing S.

Read literally, that last sentence says SA = SB, because S bisects the arc through S only when the two chords are equal. In the starting picture SA ≈ 222.16 and SB ≈ 115.66, so it is false there. The true statement, which is what the applet draws and what the valid proof of its sibling proves, is that Q is the midpoint of that arc: QA = QB and Q lies on the circle through A, B and S. The logic test confirms this on more than two thousand positions with S on the starting side of AB, and records the false sentence as false rather than quietly fixing it.

Why Q sits at the middle

By construction AD = BC and DQ = CQ, and an angle chase gives angle ADQ = angle BCQ. The two triangles ADQ and BCQ are therefore congruent, so AQ = BQ: Q lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB. A rotation about Q through the angle at S carries D to C and A to B, which puts Q on the circumcircle of ABS as well. A point of that circle equally far from A and B on the arc through S is exactly the arc's midpoint. Tick "Hint" to see the two congruent triangles and their equal side marks.

Siblings, and a faithful quirk

This is not the equilateral-triangle puzzle on segments: that one builds three triangles on AC, DC and DB and their tips line up. It is not the midpoint-rhombus applet either, or the one whose two diagonal triangles share an apex. Here one isosceles triangle has an apex angle that changes with S, and the prize is the middle of an arc. The original applet also chooses Q by a fixed turn, which gives the "away from AB" apex only while S stays on the starting side of AB. Drag S across AB and the drawn Q stops being the arc midpoint, while the other apex would be: the test checks hundreds of such positions and the status says so. This is kept as the applet behaves.

Tick Hint, then drag S around the circle. Watch Q stay on the little ring at the arc middle, then cross the segment AB to see which apex takes over.
